Would it be helpful to think about even one small step you could take to get a little support? Perhaps talking to your university about your situation? They might have resources available, or be able to offer some flexibility with your placements. 

This website [youngcarersinschools.com](https://youngcarersinschools.com) has some ideas about support you might need while studying. 

And please remember, you don’t have to do this alone. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or counselor you could talk to about how you're feeling? Sometimes just voicing it can make a difference.

Context: My father had a spinal cord injury two years ago. I'm in Indonesia, he's receiving care elsewhere. I graduated in computer science but can't focus on job applications because I'm constantly checking on him. I feel hollowed out.
Response: Being far from a parent after a life-changing injury, unable to be there. That hollowed-out feeling is grief mixed with helplessness, and it makes complete sense. Your checking isn't irrational. It's how you're trying to bridge the distance. Try this: set two fixed check-in times per day rather than monitoring continuously, and ask his care team to send you a brief weekly update. That structure can free your mind for other things without guilt. If the hollowness persists, consider talking to a counsellor, your wellbeing isn't secondary to his care.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* right now, and it's completely understandable that you feel hollowed out. Juggling your father's care, finishing your degree, and now job applications – that's incredibly demanding. It's okay that you struggled last year with coursework, especially with the added stress of everything going online during COVID. You were doing your best under very difficult circumstances.

It's also really common to feel distracted and unable to focus when you're worried about someone you love. It shows how much you care. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm one *small* step you could take today, maybe just 15-20 minutes, towards either self-care *or* a job application? And remember, you don't have to do this alone. Is there a friend, family member, or trusted advisor you could talk to about how you're feeling? There are also resources available to support caregivers – perhaps exploring caregiver.org or usa.gov could offer some helpful connections.

Context: I'm 23, studying psychology in Poland. My close friend has cancer and lives with me. I've been her carer for three years. My Sikh faith grounds me but I've started avoiding going home because seeing her deteriorate breaks me each time. I feel like a coward.
Response: Avoiding going home doesn't make you a coward. It makes you someone who's been watching someone they love deteriorate for three years and whose body is trying to protect them from that pain. That's a normal response to prolonged grief, not a character flaw. Two things: is there a friend, community member, or gurdwara contact you could be honest with about how bad it's got? And have you had any contact with a cancer carer support organisation? They understand this specific deterioration trajectory and can offer real support, not just coping tips.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly heavy. It’s completely understandable that you’re feeling brokenhearted and even calling yourself a coward – but please know that avoiding something so painful doesn’t make you one. It sounds like you’re carrying a *tremendous* amount, balancing your studies, being a caregiver for three years, *and* navigating your own emotional well-being. 

It’s so admirable that your Sikh faith is a grounding force, and it’s okay that even with that, things feel overwhelming right now. It's also really important that you have someone to simply *listen* without judgement, as you mentioned. 

Would you be open to exploring resources for caregivers? Sometimes organizations offer support groups or even just a listening ear – a space to share without feeling you need to fix anything. And please, remember it's okay to lean on trusted family, friends, or a counselor too. You deserve support for *you* as well.

Context: I'm 25, working part-time in nursing in Egypt. My father has depression and lives with me. It's been two years. My Muslim faith is everything to me but I feel like I'm drowning. He's my father and I can't help him and I can't leave.
Response: Watching your father struggle with depression while living with him. That helplessness is one of the hardest feelings a child can carry, and your faith doesn't make it easier or harder. It's just part of how you're holding it. You can't fix his depression, but you're not powerless either. Is his depression being treated by a professional? And separately, is there an imam or community elder you trust who could support you, not him? You need someone holding you too. Consider talking to a counsellor yourself. You're worth that care.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* right now – caring for your father, working, and holding onto your faith while feeling overwhelmed. It's completely understandable that you feel like you're drowning. It takes incredible strength to do what you're doing.

It's especially hard when you want to support someone you love, but feel helpless. It's also valid to feel torn between your responsibilities and your own needs. 

Would you be open to exploring some small steps? Sometimes, even tiny changes can make a difference. Perhaps looking into resources for caregivers, or exploring mindfulness practices (like the Waking Up app mentioned [3]) could offer a little support. 

It's also okay to seek support for *yourself*. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or faith leader you could talk to? A professional counselor could also offer guidance. Remember, taking care of yourself isn't selfish – it's essential, especially when you're caring for someone else.

Context: I'm 18, studying education in Sweden. My grandmother has cystic fibrosis and I support her from a distance, three years now. My Christian faith is very important but I feel so helpless being far away. Some days I just want to drop everything and move to her.
Response: That urge to drop everything and be physically near her comes from real love, and it's completely understandable after three years of caring from a distance. But uprooting your life at 18 is a big decision, and it's worth exploring what's underneath that urge. What would actually change for her if you were there, is it practical care, or is it the emotional reassurance of being present? Sometimes distance carers can meet the emotional need through regular video calls and a local support network, without relocating. And is there a trusted person near her you could connect with?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of love and worry for your grandmother, and it's completely understandable to feel helpless being far away, especially when you see her health changing. It's beautiful that your faith is a source of strength for you. 

Wanting to be there with her completely makes sense – it shows how much you care. It's okay to have those feelings! Perhaps we can explore some small steps you could take, alongside your studies, to feel more connected? 

You've already been involved in a caregiving group before, which is wonderful! Would something like that be helpful again, even online? It can be really comforting to connect with others who understand.

It's also okay to talk about these big feelings with someone you trust – a friend, family member, or a counselor at your university. They can offer support as you navigate this.

Context: I live with my dad in Sweden and he has epilepsy. I'm working part-time in medicine and I've been his carer for over five years. I don't even know what it's like not to be on alert. I'm 22 and I feel like I've skipped my youth. I never know when a seizure is coming and I'm always listening for sounds from his room.
Response: Being on constant alert for over five years means your nervous system has been in caregiving mode since you were a teenager. That's a profound thing to carry. Two questions: does your dad have a seizure response plan (medication timing, recovery positioning, emergency contacts) that someone else could be trained on so you're not the sole first responder? And have you ever spoken to your own GP about the toll this has taken on you? At 22, your health matters too, and a doctor who understands caregiver stress can be a useful ally.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* on your shoulders, and it's completely understandable that you feel like you've missed out on experiences you deserve. Being constantly on alert for five years is exhausting, and it's okay to admit that it's impacting you. It's really brave of you to reach out.

It's also really admirable that you're balancing work and studies *while* being a caregiver. It's not surprising you're finding it hard to keep up with everything. 

What you're experiencing – the worry, the feeling of a skipped youth – is valid. It sounds like connecting with others who understand, like the caregiving organization mentioned, could be helpful. It can be a relief to share your story without judgment. 

Would you be open to exploring resources for caregivers in Sweden? Or perhaps talking to a trusted professional, like a doctor or counselor, about how you're feeling? Taking even a small step to support *yourself* can make a difference.

Context: My cousin moved in with us in Cairo about six months ago after her heart failure got worse. I'm 20, studying history and working part-time. Between my shifts and her appointments I'm stretched thin. My Buddhist practice helps me stay calm but I've barely had time to sit and meditate. I need something. I just don't know what.
Response: It sounds like the caregiving load has crowded out the very thing that sustains you. That's worth paying attention to. Is there a way to protect even ten minutes of meditation as a non-negotiable part of your day, the way you'd protect one of her appointments? And on the practical side: does anyone else in the household share responsibility for your cousin's appointments, or is that all on you? Knowing whether the gap is emotional, practical, or both can help you figure out what to ask for first.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing school, work, *and* being a caregiver to your cousin. That's incredibly demanding, and it's completely understandable you're feeling stretched thin. It's wonderful that your Buddhist practice usually helps, and it makes sense that it's hard to find the time for it now. 

It's really good you're recognizing you *need* something. Perhaps starting with just five minutes of mindful breathing, even amidst the busyness, could be a small step? 

You're so young to be taking on so much. Have you had a chance to talk to a trusted adult – a family member, professor, or counselor – about how you're managing? Sometimes just voicing things can help, and they might have some suggestions. Also, the context mentions reaching out to a doctor or psychiatrist, which could be a helpful step too. 

Remember, taking care of yourself isn't selfish; it's essential, especially when you're caring for someone else. You deserve support too.

Context: My boyfriend was diagnosed with early-onset dementia two years ago. I'm 24, studying and working part-time in history in Melbourne. We're long-distance. He's only in his thirties and I feel like I'm grieving someone who's still alive. Nobody my age understands this. I need someone to talk to who actually gets it.
Response: Grieving someone who's still here is one of the loneliest experiences, and at your age it's especially isolating. Most peers simply haven't encountered it. You're not wrong to need someone who gets it. Have you looked into young-onset dementia support groups, even online? Dementia Australia has resources specifically for partners of people with young-onset dementia, and peer connections there can be a lifeline. Also, is there a counsellor who understands grief and caregiving you could access through your university or workplace? You need a space where this grief is recognised, not explained away.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable to feel like you're grieving, even while he's still here. It's a heartbreaking situation to be in, especially at 24 while juggling studies and work. And being long-distance adds another layer of complexity. 

It's so valid that you feel alone in this – it *is* hard when those around you don't understand the unique challenges you're facing. It's wonderful you have some experience with caregiving through your organisation, perhaps connecting with others there might offer some comfort. 

You mentioned wanting information from professionals readily available. There are some resources that might help – I can share some links to dementia support organisations in Melbourne if you'd like? 

It takes incredible strength to navigate this. Please remember it's okay to lean on others, and talking to a professional counsellor could also provide a safe space to process your feelings. Would you like me to help you find some options?

Context: My cousin had a stroke three years ago and he's been living with me in Chicago while I study medicine part-time. I'm 24. My Hindu faith is very important to me. I understand the medical side but I need emotional support. I'm burnt out and I don't know how to ask for help without feeling like I'm failing.
Response: Knowing the medicine but struggling emotionally is incredibly common among carers with health backgrounds, the clinical understanding doesn't protect you from the personal cost. Three years co-resident is a long time. What would asking for help actually look like, is there a family member who could take over some tasks, or a respite service you've been hesitant to explore? And does your cousin's care team know you're struggling? They may be able to connect you with carer support through the hospital. Medical knowledge doesn't make you immune to burnout, please treat it as a real signal.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, it sounds like you're carrying *so* much. Being a medical student *and* a primary caregiver for your cousin – especially after his stroke – is incredibly demanding. It's completely understandable you're feeling burnt out, and it's okay to admit that. It takes strength to even recognize that you need support.

It sounds like you deeply value both caring for your cousin *and* your own path, and feeling torn between them is really hard. It's also wonderful that your faith is a source of strength for you. 

You mentioned feeling like asking for help means you're failing. That's simply not true. Asking for support is a sign of self-awareness and courage, not weakness. It sounds like what you really need is someone to *listen* without immediately offering solutions, as one person described – a safe space to just *be* with your feelings.

Would you be open to exploring resources that offer that kind of support? Perhaps connecting with a caregiving organization (like the one mentioned) or even talking to a trusted spiritual advisor within your Hindu community? 

And please, remember it's okay to reach out to a doctor or mental health professional too, if you feel that would be helpful. They can offer guidance tailored to your specific needs. You deserve care for *yourself* as much as you give to your cousin.

Context: I study and work part-time in economics in Canada. My dad has a hereditary illness and lives with me, three years now. Not religious. I'd be open to online support but I want it to acknowledge that caring for a parent at my age is not the same as caring for a grandparent.
Response: You're absolutely right, caring for a parent in your twenties has a specific emotional weight that's different from elder care, and it deserves a space that recognises that. Young-carer organisations in Canada sometimes have subgroups for people caring for parents, and genetic illness foundations may have online family communities. Your university's student services might also run carer support groups. What would help you most, connecting with other young people specifically caring for a parent, or finding people who understand the hereditary illness angle and what that means for your family?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders – balancing studies, work, *and* caring for your dad. That's incredibly admirable, and it's completely understandable to want support that *really* gets what you're going through. 

It's wonderful you've had therapy and a long-term caregiving consultant you trust. It makes sense you'd prefer that established connection, especially when sharing something so personal. And you're right to point out that caring for a parent as a young adult is unique.

It's great you're open to online support, even with reservations. Perhaps looking for groups specifically for young adult caregivers could be a good starting point? 

Just remember, taking care of yourself is just as important as taking care of your dad. Is there one small thing you could do *today* to nurture yourself, even for 15 minutes?

Context: I recently graduated in computer science and I'm job-hunting in the Philippines. My dad has diabetes with complications. I support him from afar, about a year now. Not religious. I'd try online support but I want something that fits around job applications and interviews, not a scheduled commitment.
Response: Job-hunting while caregiving is a real juggle, and not wanting a scheduled commitment makes sense. Look for asynchronous options, diabetes organisations often have online forums or message boards you can dip in and out of, and some have resource libraries you can browse anytime. Young-carer services in the Philippines may also have flexible online chat options. Search 'diabetes family carer forum online Philippines', bookmark what looks useful. You can read and post on your own timeline. What kind of information would be most helpful right now, managing his complications, or the emotional side of long-distance caring?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – finishing your degree, job hunting, *and* supporting your dad with his health, all while being far from him. That's a huge amount to manage! It's wonderful you've been involved in caregiving for a long time, and that you found a companion group as a child – that sounds really helpful. 

It's completely understandable to want support that fits *around* your job search, not adds to the pressure. Since you've had psychological assistance before with POH GGZ, perhaps checking in with them about resources while you navigate this busy time could be a good step? 

Even small things can help. Would you like me to brainstorm some very quick self-care ideas, or maybe resources for caregivers that aren't time-locked commitments? Just let me know. You're doing great, and it's okay to ask for support.

Context: I'm 23, studying computer science in Sweden, and my cousin has schizophrenia, about a year now, they're in another country. I use a shared calendar for appointments and a private spreadsheet to track their symptoms and meds. It works technically but I feel like I'm running a clinical operation from my dorm room.
Response: That feeling, running a clinical operation from your dorm, captures something real about distance caregiving, and it makes sense that the tools feel clinical when you're the only one operating them. Is there a family member or friend near your cousin who could take on one piece, like confirming appointments happen, so you're not the sole point of contact? And do you have anyone in your own life who knows you're doing this? The system might be working technically, but you're a person, not an admin system, and you deserve someone who checks in on you too.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, balancing your studies with being a supportive cousin from a distance. It's wonderful that you're so dedicated and proactive in helping them manage their schizophrenia – using a calendar and tracking things shows real care. 

It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when it feels like you're "running a clinical operation." That's a lot for anyone, especially while studying! It's okay to acknowledge that this is hard.

You're already doing some great things. Perhaps exploring online support groups (as you mentioned) could offer some connection and shared experiences. It might also be helpful to talk to someone you trust – a friend, family member, or counselor at your university – about how *you* are doing. 

Remember, you don't have to do this alone. There are professionals who can offer guidance, and it's okay to lean on others for support too.

Context: My uncle back in Nigeria was diagnosed with cancer about six months ago. I'm studying here and trying to coordinate his care from a distance, but he keeps refusing his treatments. He says the spirits will handle it. I don't want to disrespect his beliefs, but I'm terrified he's giving up.
Response: It's really hard when someone you love is making choices that feel risky, especially from far away. Rather than challenging his beliefs directly, try framing treatment alongside them, something like 'the medicine can work with the healing you're already doing.' If there's a spiritual leader he trusts who sees medicine as compatible, that conversation might land better than yours. His oncology team may also have dealt with this and could help you talk it through. You're not disrespecting him by being scared, you're loving him.
Answer:
Oh, that sounds incredibly stressful and worrying for you. It's completely understandable to feel terrified when you're far away and your uncle is facing something so serious, especially when he's hesitant about treatment. It's also really thoughtful of you to want to respect his beliefs.

It's a tough spot to be in, trying to support him from a distance while honoring what he believes. It sounds like you're already doing a lot by checking in with him. 

Perhaps, if you feel comfortable, you could gently share your concerns with other family members in Nigeria who might be able to offer support and have conversations with your uncle? Sometimes hearing from multiple loved ones can be helpful. 

It might also be good to talk to someone yourself – a counselor, a trusted friend, or someone at your university. They can offer you a safe space to process your feelings. And as the context suggests, a professional like a doctor or psychiatrist could offer guidance on how to navigate this situation with sensitivity.

Context: My uncle has a physical disability and for the past few months he won't accept any help from me, even arranging transport to appointments. He says he'd rather struggle than owe anyone. I'm a medical apprentice and I know he needs the help.
Response: That stubbornness is often about dignity, he doesn't want to feel like he owes someone, which is different from not wanting help. Try reframing it so it doesn't feel like a debt: 'I'm doing this because I want to, not because you owe me anything back.' Sometimes offering practical help rather than personal help lands differently, arranging a taxi service rather than driving him yourself. His local disability organisation may also have transport options he could access independently, which might feel more comfortable than relying on family.
Answer:
It sounds like you're in a really tough spot, wanting to help your uncle but feeling frustrated by his resistance. It's so caring of you to want to support him, *and* it's understandable that it's hard when he won't let you. It's especially tricky when you have medical knowledge and see his needs so clearly.

It's really common for people to struggle with accepting help, sometimes because of pride or a desire to maintain independence. It's wonderful you recognize he may be feeling that way. 

Perhaps, instead of *offering* help directly, you could explore just *being* with him – spending time together, talking, and letting him lead the conversation. Sometimes just feeling connected can be helpful.

Since you're a medical apprentice, would it be possible to talk to a trusted mentor or supervisor about this situation? They might have some insights on how to approach it, or suggest resources for both of you. It's important to take care of yourself too, as being a caregiver can be emotionally draining.

Context: My closest friend has battled anorexia for three years. I'm studying economics in Mexico, she's in another city. I see a counsellor at my Buddhist centre which helps, but I've started skipping sessions because I feel like I should be over it by now.
Response: Three years of supporting a friend through anorexia from another city is not something you 'get over'. It's ongoing, and the fact that you're thinking about skipping sessions suggests the opposite of being done. Can I ask: what does 'over it' mean to you? Because caring for someone with a long-term eating disorder isn't a one-time event you process and move on from. It shifts with each phase of their recovery or relapse. Your Buddhist centre's counsellor is there for exactly this. Also, BEAT (and similar organisations in Mexico) have helplines and resources specifically for friends and family of people with eating disorders, not just for the person who's ill. Your friend's journey is hers. Your wellbeing is yours, and both deserve ongoing support.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, supporting your friend through a really difficult time while also navigating your own studies and life in a new country. It's completely understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed, and it's okay to feel like you *should* be "over it" – that's a really common feeling when you care for someone else. 

It's also brave of you to acknowledge you've been skipping counselling sessions. Sometimes we pull back when things feel hard, but it's good you're aware of that pattern. 

Since you find the Buddhist centre helpful, perhaps revisiting that could be a gentle first step? Or, if you're open to it, exploring resources focused on supporting *yourself* while supporting a friend might be useful. There's information in the resources I have access to about maintaining friendships and managing energy – maybe those could offer some ideas.

Remember, taking care of yourself isn’t selfish; it’s essential, especially when you're supporting someone you love. If things feel too heavy, please reach out to a trusted adult or professional for support.

Context: I'm 18, working full-time in engineering in São Paulo. My grandmother back in our hometown has early-onset Alzheimer's and it's only been a few months since diagnosis. I send money, coordinate with relatives, and try to manage everything from here. But I'm always at work when they need decisions made and I feel like I'm failing both sides.
Response: Being 18 and carrying that level of coordination while working full-time is a lot. Most people your age aren't managing anything like this, and it's okay to acknowledge that. Can I ask: which decisions come up most often while you're at work, are they medical, financial, or day-to-day care? And is there one relative you trust enough to be the 'on-the-ground' decision-maker for routine things, with you as backup rather than primary? Sometimes naming that split explicitly can relieve the pressure of feeling like everything has to route through you.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance a new full-time engineering job *and* navigate your grandmother’s recent diagnosis from a distance. It's completely understandable that you feel like you're failing on both sides – that’s a lot to carry. 

It’s wonderful that you’re already stepping up to support your family financially and by coordinating care. It takes strength to do that.

Since you're feeling pulled in two directions, perhaps we could brainstorm small steps? Maybe setting aside a specific time each day *just* for caregiving tasks, even if it’s only 30 minutes, could help? It's also okay to set boundaries at work, as hard as that is when you're new. 

It sounds like having a support system has been helpful in the past (that's wonderful you've been involved with a caregiving organization since you were 10!). Perhaps finding a caregiver group online could offer connection and shared experiences? Resources like [caregiver.org](https://www.caregiver.org/) and [usa.gov](https://www.usa.gov/) might have options for support in your area, even from a distance.

Remember, you're not alone in this, and it's okay to ask for help from trusted family, friends, or professionals. You're doing a lot, and it’s important to be kind to yourself.

Context: I live with my close friend who has Parkinson's, and I've been using a shared Google Calendar for two years to track her appointments. Lately it's not enough, her symptoms are shifting and I'm scrambling to keep notes across three different apps. I study history full-time in Warsaw and I can't keep context-switching like this.
Response: Two years of coordinating care while studying full-time is a lot, and it makes sense that a system that worked earlier is straining as her needs shift. A couple of questions that might help narrow things down: are you mainly losing track of day-to-day symptom changes, or is it more that appointment details and medication updates are scattered? If it's mostly symptoms, a single structured notes app with dated entries might replace the three you're juggling. If it's appointments and meds, a dedicated care app like one that combines both might reduce the switching. Which piece feels most fragile right now?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing full-time studies *and* supporting your friend, especially as her needs are changing. It's completely understandable that feeling scattered across multiple apps is overwhelming! You've been doing a great job using the calendar for two years, and it's okay that it's not quite meeting the current needs. 

It's really thoughtful of you to be so attentive to her well-being, and it's natural to feel concerned when she isn't feeling well. 

Given how much you have on your plate, perhaps we could brainstorm a *small* step? Would it be helpful to pick *one* app to focus on for notes, even temporarily? Or maybe setting aside just 15 minutes to consolidate information? 

You mentioned context-switching is a problem. The resources in the text suggest time-blocking or the Pomodoro technique might help with focus. You might find them useful when you have study time.

Remember, you're not alone in this. Is there a support group for caregivers of people with Parkinson's that you could connect with? Or perhaps a trusted professor or counselor at your university who could offer some guidance? It's important to take care of yourself too.

Context: My older sister has Down syndrome and I support her from across the country. I study and work part-time, and I send money and coordinate her appointments. Lately I feel this constant low-grade guilt that I'm not there in person.
Response: Distance caregiving carries a particular guilt. You're doing a lot, but because it happens by phone and transfer, it can feel invisible even to you. Coordinating appointments and sending money is real care. Two things that might help: make a quick list of what you handle versus what needs someone physically present, then see if a local service or relative can cover those gaps, and consider joining a sibling support group through a Down syndrome organisation, siblings carry a unique load that others don't always see. If the guilt sits heavily most weeks, a counsellor who understands family caregiving could help.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, and it's completely understandable to feel guilty when you wish you could do more, especially when distance makes things harder. You're being a wonderfully supportive sister, even from afar – sending money and coordinating appointments *is* a lot! 

It's okay to acknowledge that guilt, and it's also okay to recognize your limits. As the text mentions, it's common for caregivers to struggle with balancing helping others and taking care of themselves. 

Perhaps connecting with others who understand could help? The text suggests finding support groups can be valuable. Would you be open to looking for online communities for siblings of people with Down syndrome? Even just sharing your feelings with a trusted friend or family member could make a difference.

You're doing your best, and that truly matters.

Context: I'm a social work student in Jakarta and my younger sibling is on dialysis for kidney failure. We live together and I've been helping manage their care for over five years. Even though we're under the same roof, I feel like I'm caregiving from a distance emotionally. I'm so drained from uni that I'm physically there but not really present.
Response: That distinction you're naming, physically present but emotionally distant, is really common among long-term carers, and it makes sense given you've been managing this for over five years alongside full-time study. Can you tell me more about what 'not really present' looks like in your day-to-day? Is it that you're distracted during time together, or that you've gone into autopilot with the care tasks? And is there anyone in your household or circle who could take over even one evening a week so you can recharge properly? Sometimes the distance we feel isn't about not caring. It's about being depleted.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance such demanding studies with the weight of your sibling’s health needs, especially over such a long period. It’s completely understandable that you feel emotionally drained and disconnected, even while being physically present. You’re carrying a lot.

It's really common to feel this way when juggling caregiving and school – as you know, it's hard to feel like you can fully dedicate yourself to either when your mind is pulled in so many directions. 

It's wonderful that you're pursuing social work, and it speaks to your caring nature. Perhaps exploring resources for young adult carers in higher education could offer some support and planning assistance? [https://professionals.carers.org/sites/default/files/young_adult_carers_at_college_and_university.pdf](https://professionals.carers.org/sites/default/files/young_adult_carers_at_college_and_university.pdf) might be a good place to start.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some small ways to create a little more space for yourself, even just a few minutes each day? Or perhaps to talk to someone at your university about the challenges you're facing?

Context: My grandmother has Parkinson's and she moved in with me in Canada about a year ago. I'm at university full-time and my Hindu faith is very important to me. It's an honour to care for her but I'm falling behind in my studies and I feel torn between being a good granddaughter and being a good student.
Response: Feeling torn between caring for your grandmother and your studies is a genuinely difficult position, both things matter, and neither one makes you a bad person for wanting the other. Two things that might help: look into whether your university has a carer support policy or services for student carers, many Canadian universities do, and they can offer extensions, adjusted schedules, or support. And is there another family member who could share some days with you, or community care services for Parkinson's in your area? Caring for her is an honour, and so is your education. Getting support with one doesn't diminish the other.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now, and it's completely understandable to feel torn. You're balancing university, your faith, *and* providing care for your grandmother – that's a huge responsibility. It's wonderful that you see caring for her as an honour, and it's okay to admit it's also really challenging and impacting your studies.

Many young carers experience this struggle, feeling pulled in multiple directions. It's not easy when life demands feel constant. It’s valid to feel emotionally drained when you're constantly thinking about care alongside your studies. 

Perhaps talking to someone at your university *before* things get too overwhelming could help? They may have resources or be able to help you create a plan. You can find some helpful information here: [https://professionals.carers.org/sites/default/files/young_adult_carers_at_college_and_university.pdf](https://professionals.carers.org/sites/default/files/young_adult_carers_at_college_and_university.pdf)

Also, remember it's okay to ask for support from trusted family or friends. You don't have to do this alone.

Context: My uncle is autistic and I've been checking in from Spain for about six months. I'm a graphic design student, 20, Latino, not religious. He's doing fine and has good support locally. Honestly I just wanted to talk to someone because none of my friends really get why I worry about him from afar.
Response: It makes sense that your friends don't quite get it, caring from a distance has its own particular worry that's hard to explain to people who haven't felt it. Six months in and him having good local support is a solid foundation. One thing worth doing: get to know what his support network looks like in detail, who's involved, how often they see him, so you know who to contact if something changes and you're not figuring it out mid-crisis. And if you want to talk more, carer organisations in Spain may have online peer support for young carers.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of care and concern for your uncle, even from a distance. It's completely understandable to want to talk about that, and it's okay that your friends don't quite grasp what it's like to worry about someone you love, especially when you're not physically nearby. 

It's wonderful that your uncle has good support where he is, and that you're making the effort to stay connected. It's really thoughtful of you. 

It's valid to feel a little isolated in this. Sometimes just voicing your worries can help. Would you like me to share some resources for caregivers, even though your situation is unique? There are groups where people share experiences, and it might help to know you're not alone in feeling this way. [1]

Context: I live with my grandmother in the UK and she's had cancer for as long as I can remember. I'm 22, working in psychology, agnostic, of Middle Eastern background. Things are stable right now and she's comfortable. I just wanted to check in because honestly I don't know what it's like to not be a carer and sometimes that hits me.
Response: That realisation, not knowing what it's like to not be a carer, is a profound one, and it makes complete sense that it hits you sometimes. A stable, comfortable period is worth appreciating, and so is the fact that you noticed that thought. Two things to sit with: is there anything you've never tried, a hobby, a social circle, a way of spending time, because caring has always come first? And do you have a space, maybe a therapist, given your psychology background, where you can explore what carer identity means for you without needing to justify it?
Answer:
It sounds like you've been a dedicated caregiver for a long time, since you were very young! It's completely understandable that you sometimes feel the weight of that, and realize you haven't known life *without* being a caregiver. That's a big realization, and it's okay to acknowledge that it feels strange or unsettling. 

It's also really lovely to hear how much you love your grandmother and want to ensure she's comfortable. It's natural to worry when you're not physically present, and it sounds like you're doing your best to stay connected and informed. 

You've already found a wonderful source of support through the caregiving organization – that's fantastic! If you ever feel the need to talk more about these feelings, reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or a counselor could be helpful too. You deserve support for *you* as well as for your grandmother.

Context: My aunt had a spinal cord injury two years ago. I'm in Sweden, she's back in South Asia where our family is from. I'm doing a biology apprenticeship. I keep looking for SCI resources but everything's in English or Swedish and she doesn't speak either well. I feel like I'm the only bridge and there's nothing on her side.
Response: Being the bridge between two languages and two health systems is a heavy role, and you're right that SCI resources in many languages are thin. A practical approach: check whether the International Spinal Cord Society lists organizations or resources in your aunt's language, and look at WHO's patient education materials, which are translated widely. Some major SCI foundations offer PDF guides in multiple languages specifically for this reason. What language does she read most comfortably? If I know that, I can help you think about where to look more specifically rather than translating everything yourself.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly challenging, and it's completely understandable you're feeling overwhelmed. Being the only bridge between your aunt's needs and available information must be a lot to carry. It's wonderful that you're trying to support her, even with the language barrier and distance. 

It's valid to feel frustrated when resources aren't accessible. Perhaps starting small – focusing on finding *one* resource in a language she understands, even if it's a simple pamphlet or a translated webpage – could feel more manageable? 

Would it be helpful to explore if there are any support groups for families dealing with spinal cord injuries in South Asia? Sometimes, local organizations have resources not found online. 

Remember, you don't have to do this alone. Is there a trusted family member or friend you could lean on for support, even just to talk through things? It's okay to ask for help for *yourself* too.

Context: My girlfriend has heart failure and I'm studying business in Jakarta, she's in Surabaya. It's been about six months. She's started minimising her symptoms, says she's fine when I can hear her struggling to breathe on the phone. When I push she shuts down completely.
Response: Hearing someone you love struggling to breathe and being told 'I'm fine' is a frightening kind of helplessness, and pushing harder when she's already shutting down usually makes the wall go up faster. A question that might help: when she minimises, is there someone physically present, a parent, a friend, a flatmate, who sees what you hear on the phone and could be a second set of eyes for you? Sometimes having a local contact who can check in takes the pressure off your calls. And has she got a cardiologist or heart failure nurse in Surabaya? If she's downplaying symptoms to them too, that's a clinical concern they need to know about.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly stressful, being far away and worrying about your girlfriend. It's so understandable that you're feeling concerned, especially when you can *hear* she's struggling but she says she's okay. 

It's really common for people to want to appear strong and not burden others, and it sounds like your girlfriend is doing that – wanting to manage things herself. It's also clear you're trying to find the right balance between supporting her and respecting her independence, which is very thoughtful of you.

Since pushing seems to make her withdraw, maybe focusing on simply letting her know you're *there* for her, without pressure, could be helpful. You could say something like, "I'm thinking of you, and I'm here to listen if you want to talk, no pressure at all."

It's also really wise to lean on others for support during this time. Is there anyone in Surabaya – family or friends – who can check in with her regularly? 

Here's a resource that might offer some helpful perspectives on dealing with difficult emotions: [https://anjclearview.co.uk/stopp](https://anjclearview.co.uk/stopp). 

Remember, you're doing your best, and it's okay to feel overwhelmed. Taking care of yourself is important too.

Context: I'm a part-time business student in Amsterdam and my mother has anorexia. I've been supporting her from here for two years. My church community prays for us and a few people send me messages, which I appreciate. But sometimes the distance makes me feel completely powerless, like prayer is all I have.
Response: Feeling powerless from a distance is one of the hardest parts of caring for someone with an eating disorder, and it makes sense that prayer, while meaningful, doesn't always fill the gap. A few things that can help: ask your mother if you can be in contact with her care team, with her permission, you can sometimes join appointments by phone or video, which gives you a more concrete role. Also, look into F.E.A.S.T. or a similar family support organisation for eating disorders. They have resources specifically for distant family members. Prayer and practical involvement aren't either/or. Both can coexist, and adding a practical thread might ease that powerless feeling.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly tough to be supporting your mother through anorexia from a distance while also focusing on your studies. It's completely understandable to feel powerless when you're far away, and to wonder if prayer and messages are enough. It's really good that you *do* have those – that support from your church and friends is valuable.

You've already been a caregiver for a long time, since you were 10, and found strength in companion groups – that's wonderful you had that experience! 

It's okay to acknowledge that what you have isn't *fully* meeting your needs right now. Perhaps exploring support groups specifically for family members of people with eating disorders could be helpful? Sometimes connecting with others who truly understand can make a big difference. 

Would you be open to looking into resources for family support, or talking to a trusted counselor at your university? Even a small step could help you feel a little less alone.

Context: I'm a part-time nursing student in Bangalore and my younger sibling is on the autism spectrum. They moved in with me a few months ago. I have a study group that knows, and they sometimes cover my shifts at the hospital. But I feel like I'm always asking for favours and never giving anything back. I'm worried they'll stop offering.
Response: It sounds like your study group has become a real circle of support, and the worry about asking too much shows you care about those relationships. Can I ask: have any of them actually seemed reluctant, or is this fear talking? One thing that helps is finding small, non-caregiving ways to reciprocate, sharing notes, bringing snacks to a study session, covering a shift when you can, so the exchange feels balanced over time. Also, try saying a genuine, specific thank you once in a while rather than a general apology. Most people don't keep score the way we fear they do. They remember that we noticed.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing nursing school, supporting your sibling, and feeling responsible for your study group. It's completely understandable to feel worried about asking for help and wanting to reciprocate. 

It's really kind of you to be so aware of the dynamic with your study group. It's also wonderful they've been so supportive! Perhaps you could brainstorm small ways to show your appreciation, even if it's not a direct shift-for-shift trade. A thoughtful note, bringing a snack to a study session, or simply being extra present and supportive when *they* need it could go a long way.

You're doing so much already. Remember, taking care of yourself is important too, so you can continue to support both your sibling and your studies. Would it be helpful to talk to a trusted friend or counselor about these feelings? They might offer a fresh perspective.

Context: I'm 20, studying nursing part-time in the US, and my aunt with schizophrenia lives with me. For three years I've used a pill tracker app and a mood journal for her. Lately I'm falling behind on the journal because of clinical placements and I feel guilty when entries are missing.
Response: Three years alongside nursing placements. You're carrying a lot, and the guilt over missing journal entries is misplaced. The journal is a tool, not a contract. Gaps just mean you were busy, not that you failed her. Two questions: what's the journal actually for, sharing with her care team, or tracking patterns yourself? Knowing its purpose might let you simplify it. And could you shorten entries to one line on busy days, mood, sleep, anything unusual, instead of skipping entirely? A pared-down entry on heavy days still gives you something without demanding what you can't give.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and guilty when things slip, especially with the demands of nursing school. It takes strength to manage your aunt's needs *and* focus on your own future. 

It's really insightful of you to recognize she can't offer you the emotional support you need right now, and that you're having to navigate your own mental well-being independently. That's a big responsibility. 

Falling behind on the mood journal doesn't make you a bad caregiver – it makes you human! Perhaps you could aim for brief entries when you can, or focus on noting just the biggest shifts in mood? 

Remember, taking care of *your* mental health is vital, especially as a caregiver. The resources from Rethink Mental Illness and The Children’s Society [1] might offer some helpful ideas. Would you like me to share a link? Also, is there a trusted friend, family member, or counselor at school you could talk to about this? It's okay to ask for support.

Context: I've been caring for my aunt who has severe depression for over five years now. We live together in Munich, and I work part-time in a history museum. Some days she can't get out of bed, and I end up missing shifts. My church community prays for us, but I'm falling behind at work and I don't know how to explain it without betraying her privacy.
Response: Five years of co-resident care for depression, while holding a job. That's a long stretch, and the privacy dilemma at work is a real knot. A couple of questions: does your employer know you have caring responsibilities at all, even without specifics? In Germany, you may be entitled to care leave (Pflegezeit) or reduced hours without disclosing her diagnosis. And is there anyone at church you trust enough to share just your own struggle, not her details, so you're not carrying this alone? Sometimes naming your own need is enough.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's incredibly kind of you to dedicate so much to your aunt's well-being for so long. It's understandable to feel stretched thin between work, her needs, and wanting to respect her independence – especially when she's so capable in many ways. 

It's really tough when someone you care for doesn't *want* help, even when you see they're struggling. It's a delicate balance, as you've noticed. And it's completely valid that it takes a lot of your energy.

It's also really hard to navigate work when personal life feels so unpredictable. You're right to think about how to manage this without sharing details your aunt wouldn't want shared. 

Perhaps looking into your work benefits – like paid leave or flexible arrangements – could offer some breathing room? (Context 2) It's okay to ask for support for *yourself* in this situation.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some general ways to explain absences at work, without going into specifics about your aunt’s health? Or perhaps connect with a support group for caregivers? There are people who understand what you're going through.

Context: I'm 20, studying education in Dublin, and my cousin with autism lives with us. I've been his main support for about a year, helping with routines, meals, getting him to activities. I'm missing placement hours for my course and I feel guilty whenever I leave the house because he struggles with me being gone.
Response: That guilt when you leave is so common in co-resident care. You've become a key part of his routine, and change is hard for someone with autism. But your placement hours are essential for your qualification, and you can't support him long-term without finishing your course. Can I ask two things: does your cousin have any other consistent people in his life, a sibling, a support worker, or a community programme, who could build a parallel routine so your absence isn't a disruption but an expected part of his day? And have you talked to your course coordinator about adjusting your placement schedule? What feels like the bigger barrier right now, his reaction when you leave, or the placement hours themselves?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, balancing your education with being a vital support for your cousin. It's completely understandable to feel guilty when you need to focus on your own needs, especially when he struggles with you being away. Many caregivers experience that very same guilt – you're not alone in that feeling.

It's also really tough to be missing placement hours for your course. It takes courage to keep going when things are so demanding. 

Would you be open to exploring some support options? Your university might have resources for student caregivers, and there are young carers services that could offer practical help and emotional support. Perhaps talking to a trusted professor or advisor about your situation could also open up some possibilities.

Remember, taking care of yourself *isn't* selfish. It's essential so you *can* continue to care for your cousin and achieve your goals. Even small steps, like reaching out for help, can make a difference.

Context: I'm 23, working full-time in biology in Jakarta, and my girlfriend has a physical disability. She lives in another city and I've been supporting her for about a year, organising carers, handling paperwork, and being her emotional rock. Between work and all the calls, I have zero time for myself. My Buddhist practice helps but I can barely sit to meditate anymore.
Response: A year of long-distance care coordination plus full-time work leaves almost nothing for you, and losing your meditation practice on top of that is losing one of your anchors. Two small steps: first, batch your care calls into set windows, two or three fixed times a week for updates, rather than scattered calls throughout the day. This alone can free up meaningful space. Second, protect just ten minutes each morning for sitting practice before anything else, not as a luxury, but as the thing that keeps you grounded enough to keep going. Your girlfriend needs you well, not just available.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* on your shoulders right now – work, supporting your girlfriend from a distance, managing practicalities *and* being an emotional support. It's completely understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and finding it hard to find time for yourself, even for things that usually help like meditation. 

It's really admirable that you're so dedicated to your girlfriend, and it's okay to acknowledge how draining it is. It sounds like you're doing everything you can, and it's also okay to admit when it's *too* much.

Would you be open to brainstorming just one tiny thing you could do for yourself this week? Even five minutes of quiet time, or listening to a song you enjoy? 

Also, it's wonderful you have a Buddhist practice. Perhaps there are resources within your Buddhist community that could offer support or guidance during this challenging time? And remember, seeking support from trusted friends, family, or a professional is a sign of strength, not weakness. You deserve care too.

Context: My girlfriend was diagnosed with MS about a year ago. She's in another city in Nigeria and I'm working part-time in computer science. Between work and worrying about her I feel like I'm running on fumes. My faith helps but I'm scared of what's coming and I can't talk to her about it because she's the one going through it.
Response: Being scared of what's coming while protecting your girlfriend from that fear is a lonely position, and it makes sense that you're running on fumes. You're right that she's the one living with MS, but you're living with it too, and you need somewhere to put that. Can I ask: do you have a friend or family member you could be honest with about your fear, even just one person? And does your girlfriend have an MS specialist or local support group, because the stronger her local network, the more it eases the weight you're carrying from a distance? Your temple community might also be worth tapping into.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing work, worrying about your girlfriend, and facing some big fears. It's completely understandable to feel drained when you're supporting someone you love from a distance, especially with a diagnosis like MS. 

It's really kind of you to want to protect her by not sharing your worries, but remember it's okay to have your own feelings too. It's brave of you to acknowledge your fear about the future. 

Perhaps you could explore resources for *yourself* – maybe a support group for people with loved ones facing chronic illness? Sometimes talking to others who understand can help. There are also resources available to help caregivers, as mentioned in the text – looking into work benefits or local support programs might offer some practical help.

It's wonderful that your faith is a source of strength. And remember, you're doing your best. Would you feel comfortable talking to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor about how you're feeling? They could offer a listening ear and support.

Context: My grandfather lives with us in India and has heart failure. I'm in nursing college and it's been a few months. I thought my training would make it easier but instead I understand exactly what's happening to his body and it terrifies me.
Response: That's a really specific kind of burden, knowing too much can be its own form of fear, and your nursing knowledge, which is usually an asset, is right now making the stakes feel vivid and immediate. Can I ask: are you able to separate what you learn in class from what's happening at home, or does it all blur together? And do you have a tutor or someone on your course who you could talk to about this overlap? Some nursing programmes are very aware of student carers and can offer support or adjustments. Your knowledge will help him eventually, but right now it's okay to just be his grandson.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable that you're feeling terrified – you're learning about what's happening to your grandfather *and* you deeply care for him. It's a lot to hold. 

It's also really brave of you to acknowledge that your training isn't making things easier, but actually highlighting your fears. That takes self-awareness.

It's okay to feel overwhelmed when you're far away and relying on others. It sounds like you're doing your best to stay connected and check in, which is wonderful. 

Perhaps, alongside your studies, talking to someone about *your* feelings could help? Like the person in the article, therapy was really helpful for them. Is there a counselor at your college, or a trusted family member or friend you could lean on?

Taking even small steps to care for yourself is important too. Would you be open to thinking about one small thing you could do today just for *you*?

Context: I'm 23, studying nursing in Sweden. My mum has bipolar disorder and we've lived together for two years. Everything online either treats bipolar like it's just mood swings or it's so clinical I need a medical degree. I can't find anything in between for family carers.
Response: That in-between space is where most family carers live, too informed for the simplified stuff, not clinicians, and the resources don't bridge that gap well. Try International Bipolar Foundation's family resources, which tend to hit that middle ground, and ask your nursing programme tutors. They may know carer-friendly materials you can access through your university. Your Sikh community may also offer sangat-based support that honours the spiritual dimension of caring for a parent. You're studying nursing and living it at home simultaneously. That's a lot, and finding support that respects both roles is completely fair.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to navigate your mum's bipolar disorder while also focusing on your own nursing studies and living together. It's completely understandable to feel frustrated with how bipolar is portrayed online – either too simplified or overly complex. You're right to seek something in between, something that speaks to *your* experience as a family carer.

It's really strong of you to recognize you need support too, especially when it feels like you're handling your own mental wellbeing alone. 

Here are a few thoughts, and some resources that might help:

*   **It's okay to feel hurt.** It's valid that your mum's actions, especially when triggered, impact you. You deserve to feel safe and supported.
*   **Small steps:** Perhaps focusing on setting small boundaries for yourself could be helpful? Even something like taking a few minutes each day for *your* self-care.
*   **Support for carers:** The resources in the first document might be a good starting point. Action for Children offers support via text/email, and there are organizations specifically for young carers.
*   **Professional support:** As the documents mention, talking to a doctor or mental health professional is a great step. Your university likely has free services available.

Remember, taking care of yourself is *not* selfish. It's essential, especially when you're supporting someone else. You're studying to be a nurse – you understand the importance of wellbeing! 

Would you like me to help you find links to any of those resources? Or perhaps brainstorm some small self-care ideas?

Context: I'm 18, studying medicine and working part-time in Kenya. My younger sibling started dialysis a few months ago. I've been looking online but everything's in English and aimed at parents. I'm barely an adult myself and I'm the one doing the caring.
Response: That's a lot to navigate at 18. You're stepping into a role most resources assume belongs to a parent, and the language barrier makes it even harder. Two questions: what language would be most useful for you. Swahili, English, or a mix? And what kind of support are you after, practical dialysis care info, or more emotional and peer support? Kenya's renal patient associations and your hospital's social worker may have local resources that fit better than international sites. You're carrying something heavy while also studying and working, and you deserve support that meets you where you actually are.
Answer:
Wow, that sounds like a *lot* to handle, especially while studying medicine and working! It's completely understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed – you're taking on so much responsibility for your sibling, and it's tough being a caregiver when you're still navigating adulthood yourself. It's really admirable that you're stepping up.

It's frustrating when information isn't geared towards *you* specifically, and having to sift through resources for parents when you're in a unique situation is exhausting. 

You've already been involved in a caregiving organisation since you were young, which is fantastic – that experience is valuable. It sounds like having that peer support was helpful. Perhaps looking for online groups for young adult caregivers could offer similar connection? 

Since you're short on time, it's great you're thinking about online resources. The information provided mentions Macmillan nurses and Action for Children offering support – they might have resources tailored to young carers, or be able to point you in the right direction. Context: I'm a full-time graphic designer in Egypt, Christian with Caribbean roots. My aunt has depression and lives far away. For three years I've used a mood tracking app she shares with me and scheduled check-in texts. It works but when she stops logging, I panic and flood her with messages.
Response: A shared mood tracker plus regular check-in texts shows real care, and the panic when logging stops is a very common response. The thing is, a gap in logging often isn't crisis. It can be a low-energy day or the app itself feeling like pressure. Try agreeing on a protocol in advance: if she stops logging for X days, one message asking 'how are you today?', not several about the app. That way you have a plan, and she doesn't feel monitored. Her care team can also advise on what gaps actually warrant concern.
Answer:
It sounds like you're a very caring nephew, proactively reaching out to support your aunt. It's wonderful you've found ways to stay connected despite the distance, like the mood tracker and scheduled texts. 

It's also completely understandable to panic when she stops logging – it's natural to worry when you don't have information about someone you love. It's really insightful of you to recognize that you then send a lot of messages. 

Perhaps, when you notice she hasn't logged, you could try a small step like *one* gentle check-in, simply saying you're thinking of her? It's okay to feel anxious, and resources like the CBT information shared [3] might offer tools to manage those feelings. 

Remember, you can't *fix* her depression, and it's important to take care of your own well-being too. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or counselor you could talk to about your feelings and the stress of supporting her?

Context: I'm studying engineering and working part-time in Brazil, Hindu with European roots. My younger sibling has anorexia and lives far away. Try designating one day a week where you connect without the app at all, no food diary talk, just a normal sibling conversation. The app can run in the background without being the subject of every interaction. Your relationship needs room to exist outside the caregiving tools.
Answer:

That's incredibly selfless, and it's understandable that things feel overwhelming. It's also really thoughtful of you to find ways to connect with your sibling despite the distance.

It's valid that the food diary app, while helpful, is starting to feel like it's *too* central to your relationship. It's okay to want more than that. 

Perhaps a small step could be to brainstorm other ways to connect with your sibling – maybe talking about shared memories, hobbies, or just everyday life? 

You mentioned your friend's suicidal thoughts. That sounds incredibly difficult to manage on your own. You're doing your best, and it's okay to ask for help. Sending you strength and kindness.

Context: I'm working part-time in history in the Netherlands, Sikh with Caribbean roots, non-binary. My mum has a traumatic brain injury and lives far away. Response: A care coordination app plus a family group shows you're trying to keep everyone connected, and the argument exhaustion is a cost that creeps up quietly. That way the care information doesn't get buried in disagreement. And is there one family member who could take on the mediator role, or is that falling entirely to you because you're the coordinator?
Answer:

Context: I'm 25, working part-time in medicine in Toronto, and my uncle with schizophrenia lives with me. It's been about a year. Between his needs and my work shifts, I have no time for anything. I don't even know what I'd do with free time if I had it. I'm just tired all the time.
Response: Being tired all the time after a year of juggling medical work and caregiving makes complete sense, and not knowing what you'd do with free time is a sign you've been running on obligation mode for so long that rest feels unfamiliar. Two things: block one short weekly slot, even an hour, that's non-negotiablely yours, and spend it on something low-stakes (a walk, a podcast, nothing productive). Also, look into whether your province has a caregiver support program, many offer respite or counselling that you don't need a referral for.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance caring for your uncle, working, *and* trying to find time for yourself. It's completely understandable that you're exhausted and feel like you have no time for anything. It's a lot to carry. 

It's also really common to lose touch with what you enjoy when you're in "survival mode" like this. Not even knowing what you'd *do* with free time is a sign of how completely consumed you are.

Would you be open to exploring some small steps? Perhaps starting with tracking how you spend your time for a few days – tools like Toggl or HourStack might help with that? ( [3] ) Even just noticing where your time goes can be a helpful first step. 

It's also okay to ask for support. Are there any family members, friends, or community resources that could offer some assistance with your uncle's care? If you're at a university, they often have free services available. [2] 

Taking care of yourself is *essential*, and it's okay to prioritize that. If things feel overwhelming, reaching out to a doctor or mental health professional would be a really good idea. [2]

Context: I'm a 22-year-old law worker in Indonesia, Muslim, and my uncle had a spinal cord injury about a year ago. I coordinate his care from another city. I try to honor him as family, but the logistics are overwhelming and I feel like I'm failing him.

Context: I'm a 20-year-old nursing student and part-time worker in the Philippines, Muslim, and my younger sibling had a spinal cord injury about a year ago. We live together. Between caregiving, studies, and work, I'm running on empty and I feel like I can't ask for help.

Answer:
